Field surveys of Nanorana taihangnica in the Taihangshan region have provided detailed morphometric data across the life cycle. Newly deposited eggs, characterized by a diameter of approximately 3.63 millimeters, yield an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.000025 grams [Wwb = 0.000025 grams], representing the initial mass of the endotrophic tadpole prior to the onset of exogenous feeding. The free-swimming larva grows steadily, and at metamorphic climax, following completion of tail resorption and limb development, the recently metamorphosed froglet attains a snout-vent length of 3.6 centimeters . Concurrently, the wet weight at metamorphosis reaches 4.2 grams , a value that reflects the substantial mass gain achieved during the aquatic larval phase. These early-life measurements serve as critical baseline data for understanding the energetic investment required to reach the terrestrial juvenile stage.

The transition to a reproductively viable adult involves distinct growth trajectories that differ between sexes. For females, sexual maturation occurs at a snout-vent length of 6.4 centimeters [Lp = 6.4 centimeters], a size that corresponds to the attainment of gonadal maturity and the capacity for egg deposition. Males, in contrast, reach puberty at a smaller body size of 5.3 centimeters [Lp = 5.3 centimeters], reflecting a well-documented pattern of sexual size dimorphism observed across many amphibian taxa. The wet weight at puberty for males is recorded at 11.2 grams [Wwp = 11.2 grams], while females, by the time they achieve reproductive maturity, have accumulated a substantially greater mass of 23.7 grams [Wwp = 23.7 grams]. This disparity in mass at maturity likely reflects the greater energetic requirements associated with oogenesis and the production of yolk-laden eggs.

Under the cool montane conditions typical of the species' habitat, maintained at a constant temperature of 11 °C [T = 11 °C], the developmental chronology of Nanorana taihangnica is notably prolonged. Female reproductive output in Nanorana taihangnica is characterized by a single annual breeding event that occurs under the same thermal regime. At 11 °C [T = 11 °C], each gravid female produces a clutch containing between 302 and 611 eggs [N_R_i = each gravid female produces a clutch containing between 302 and 611 eggs], with a single clutch produced each year [F_R_i = single clutch produced each year]. This annual reproductive frequency is typical of temperate-zone ranid frogs that experience a distinct breeding season constrained by the duration of suitable thermal conditions. The maximum adult body size that females ultimately achieve is a snout-vent length of 9.2 centimeters [Li = 9.2 centimeters], which allows for the accommodation of substantial clutch volumes within the body cavity. Males, following a different growth trajectory, achieve a smaller ultimate snout-vent length of 8.2 centimeters [Li = 8.2 centimeters], a difference that underscores the selective pressures driving dimorphism in this species.

The upper bound of physiological longevity in this species has been estimated from mark-recapture studies in the Taihangshan Mountains under prevailing thermal conditions. At a field temperature of 11 °C [T = 11 °C], the lifespan of Nanorana taihangnica is approximately 3650 days [am = approximately 3650 days], equating to roughly ten years. This relatively extended lifespan for a frog of its size is consistent with the slow life-history pace conferred by cool environments and delayed maturation. In terms of adult body mass, sexually mature females attain an ultimate wet weight of 70.4 grams [Wwi = 70.4 grams], which is nearly double the 41.4 grams [Wwi = 41.4 grams] recorded as the ultimate wet weight for adult males. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism in both structural length and mass has direct consequences for reproductive output, as larger females are capable of producing larger clutches and thus contribute disproportionately to population recruitment.
